scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Gnawa music emerged in Morocco from traditions of enslaved West Africans displaced through the trans-Saharan slave trade between the 11th and 17th centuries.
The population originates from a broad region extending from Senegal to Chad and from Mali to Southern Nigeria, maintaining historical links with the royal Black Guard of Morocco.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Performances occur during lila or derdeba, all-night communal ceremonies of prayer, sacrifice, and healing held from late evening until sunrise.
The ritual aims to reintegrate and balance the main powers of the human body through engagement with spiritual entities.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The ceremony begins with an opening consecration known as the aâda, where musicians perform a swirling acrobatic dance while playing the krakeb castanets.
During the lila, participants enter an ecstatic trance state called jedba, performing specialized dances corresponding to the seven families of mluk spirits.
Watch for Aâda opening dance.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Central instruments include the hajhuj (also called guembri or sentir), a three-stringed lute played with a drop-thumb frailing technique, and the qraqab (krakeb), heavy iron castanets.
Rural settings also utilize large tbel drums, while melodies emphasize the tonic and fifth with pitch-flattening around the third and seventh degrees.
Listen for the qraqab, krakeb, hajhuj, guembri.
The pulse is interplay between triple and duple meters.
Throbbing bass drone from the guembri's freely vibrating string combined with the metallic, telegraphic percussive patterns of iron krakeb castanets and repeating vocal chants.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Prominent maâlems include Mahmoud Gania ('the King'), Hamid El Kasri, H'mida Boussou, Chérif Regragui, Allal Soudani, Abdellah El Gourd, and Abdeslam Alikkane, many of whom have bridged traditional rituals with international jazz and world music collaborations.
Maâlems often blend regional styles, such as Gharbaoui from Rabat, Marsaoui from Essaouira, and Soussi or Berber styles from southern Morocco, combining local musical flavors into their repertoire.
Gnawa maintains spiritual and musical ties to West African traditions such as the Hausa halam lute, while existing as a distinct Moroccan Sufi brotherhood tradition recognized by UNESCO.

scenes.title: A respectful note
narration: Gnawa features sacred possession rituals (jedba and lila) involving spiritual entities (mluk) and animal sacrifice; outsiders must respect the spiritual boundaries of these healing ceremonies.

music_brief.prompt: Original instrumental composition in the musical world of Gnawa (Morocco). Meter interplay between triple and duple meters. Rhythm pattern: seven musical patterns, seven melodic and rhythmic cells. Instruments: qraqab, krakeb, hajhuj, guembri, gimbri, sentir, tbel, gogo. Vocal style: short call-response refrains, repeating phrases. Form: suites for specific mluk spirits. Mood: trance, healing, ecstatic, hypnotic. It should sound like this: Throbbing bass drone from the guembri's freely vibrating string combined with the metallic, telegraphic percussive patterns of iron krakeb castanets and repeating vocal chants. New melody, new arrangement: do not quote or imitate any specific recorded song; keep the idiom, the instruments, the pulse and the proportions.
